transcript.text: We had a power cut last night and now our Candy washer dryer is completely dead - no lights, nothing. Everything else in the house came back on. The plug fuse is fine, I swapped it. Help!

A power cut followed by a dead machine usually comes down to one of three things, roughly in this order: the supply to that particular socket hasn't actually come back (often a separate switched/fused spur or its own breaker), the mains suppressor/filter inside the machine (the first part that sees the power, and the one most often hit by a surge when the power returns), or, less often, the power-supply section of the main control board. Swapping the plug fuse was the right first step, so the next job is to prove the socket before we blame the machine. 1. Plug something simple like a kettle or lamp into the same socket the washer-dryer uses. If that's dead too, the problem is the house supply to that socket, not the machine.
2. Look for a switched fused spur near the socket or in a cupboard (a switch plate, sometimes with a small fuse holder, often labelled washer). Make sure it's switched on. These spurs have their own fuse, which can blow on a surge even when everything else in the house is fine.
3. Check the consumer unit (fuse box) for any single breaker or RCBO that's down. Kitchen appliance circuits are sometimes on their own breaker, so one can stay off while the rest of the house comes back.
4. Unplug the machine for 10 to 15 minutes, then plug it back in firmly. If it has a programme dial, turn it to Off and then to a programme. This lets the electronics fully reset after the outage. If the socket works with another appliance, any spur and breaker are on, and the washer-dryer is still completely dead after that reset, the fault is inside the machine. The mains suppressor/filter would be my first suspect, ahead of the control board. Confirming that means taking the top cover off and testing it unplugged, which is a job for a competent DIYer or an engineer. If you notice any burning smell, or the house electrics trip when you plug it in, leave it unplugged and get an engineer. So, does the socket work with something else, and is there a spur switch for it?

Yes, the socket works - I plugged a lamp in and it's fine. Consumer unit is all on, and I unplugged the machine for over 10 minutes and tried again but it's still dead. Not sure about a spur switch, I haven't seen one.

[Heading: Likely cause: mains filter]
That's really useful. With the socket proven by the lamp, the breakers all on, a good plug fuse and a proper reset done, the house supply is ruled out, so the fault is inside the machine. On the spur: if the lamp works in that same socket, whatever feeds it is on. My main suspect is the mains suppressor, also called the mains filter. It's the first part the incoming power reaches, and it's the one most often damaged when the power surges back after a cut. Less likely is a burnt connection in the incoming wiring. The control board's power-supply section comes last, and it's only worth suspecting once the filter and wiring are cleared. I'd put the filter well ahead, though I can't be certain without it being tested. A mains filter is usually a fairly cheap, quick part to swap. It normally sits just under the top cover at the back where the mains lead comes in. It needs testing and replacing with the machine unplugged, so it's a job for a competent DIYer with a multimeter, or an engineer. If you'd like me to help find the right part, I'll need the model number. It's usually on a sticker around the door rim (open the door and look round the opening) or on the back of the door glass surround. If you can't get to it right now, that's fine, it can wait. While it's dead, keep it unplugged. If you notice any burning smell or scorch marks near where the lead goes in, leave it for an engineer.
[Panel: "To check a suitable replacement — Enter your model number below. Once we have the model I can check whether a suitable replacement is available. It's usually on a sticker inside the door or around the frame, or on the back of the appliance."]
The model number on the label is CSOW 4965TWE/1-80. It's a Candy Smart Pro, about 3 years old. I won't be taking any panels off myself though.

[Heading: Likely cause: mains filter]
That's completely reasonable. Since this fix sits under the top cover, an engineer is the right route rather than a DIY job. On the part: I couldn't find a confirmed parts match for CSOW 4965TWE/1-80, so I don't want to point you at a filter that might not fit. 1. Book a Candy (Haier) service engineer through the manufacturer's website, quoting the full model number from the label. They'll have the correct parts listed against it.
2. Or use a local independent appliance engineer. That points them straight at the incoming power path (mains filter first, then the incoming wiring, then the board's power supply), which should keep the call-out short. Before you book, it's worth checking a few things at about three years old. Some Candy models came with an extended guarantee, and home insurance, an appliance cover plan or a credit-card purchase can sometimes cover surge damage from a power cut. One quick thing you can do yourself while it's unplugged is look along the mains lead and plug for any kinks, crush damage or scorching. Anything like that is worth mentioning to the engineer. On cost: if it's the mains filter, as I suspect, it's normally a cheap part and a quick job, so it's well worth repairing on a three-year-old machine. It only gets closer to a repair-or-replace decision if the engineer finds the control board has been damaged too, so ask them for a price before they fit a board. Until then, keep it unplugged.

candidates: Supply to the machine not restored (dead socket, switched/fused spur off or its fuse blown, or a tripped breaker on that (medium)
Mains interference suppressor/filter damaged by the power cut or surge (medium)
Control PCB power-supply section damaged by the surge (low)
